title: White Grapes and Their Places
description: The principal white grapes, the regions that made them famous and how place changes the wine.
L: Name Chardonnay's classic regions in Burgundy
Compare cool and warm climate Chardonnay
Recognise the effect of oak and malolactic

Chardonnay comes from Burgundy, where it makes almost all the white wine. Chablis, in the cool north, gives lean, steely wines with green apple and lemon, often unoaked. The Côte de Beaune, with Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, gives richer, nutty wines fermented and aged in oak. The Mâconnais, further south, gives rounder, fruitier, good-value wines.
Chablis: steely. Côte de Beaune: rich.

Chardonnay grows almost everywhere. In warm places like California's Central Valley or parts of Australia it gives tropical fruit, high alcohol and often lots of oak. Cooler sites, like Sonoma Coast, Tasmania, Adelaide Hills or Limarí in Chile, now make tighter, fresher styles. Since the 2000s, many producers have cut back on new oak and malolactic.
Cool sites: citrus. Warm sites: tropical.
Which Burgundy area is known for lean, steely, often unoaked Chardonnay?
Chablis is the coolest part of Burgundy, and its wines are typically crisp and mineral. Meursault is richer and oaked.

Chardonnay takes winemaking well. Barrel fermentation and new oak add vanilla and toast. Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into soft lactic acid, adding a buttery note. Lees stirring gives a creamy texture. Unoaked versions are fresh and fruity. The label rarely tells you which, but the region and price are good clues.
Oak, malolactic and lees shape the style
Which flavours suggest a warm-climate, oaked Chardonnay?
Tropical fruit comes from heat; vanilla, toast and butter from oak and malolactic. Green apple and lime point to a cool climate.
Burgundy is Chardonnay's home: Chablis lean, the Côte de Beaune rich
Cool sites give citrus; warm sites give tropical fruit
Oak, malolactic and lees add toast, butter and cream
Compare Loire and Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc
Explain where green and tropical aromas come from

Sauvignon Blanc's classic home is the Loire's Central Vineyards, mainly Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. Their cool climate and chalky or flinty soils give high acidity, citrus, green apple and a smoky, stony character. The wines are usually unoaked and restrained.

Marlborough, in New Zealand, put Sauvignon on the world map in the 1980s with intense passion fruit, gooseberry and cut grass. Sunny days and cold nights give ripe fruit and high acidity together. The green notes come from pyrazines; the tropical notes from thiols, released during fermentation. Machine harvesting and skin contact can increase them.
Which compounds give Sauvignon Blanc its green, grassy aromas?
Pyrazines give grass and green pepper. Thiols give passion fruit and grapefruit. Terpenes are the floral compounds of Muscat and Riesling.

In Bordeaux, Sauvignon is blended with Sémillon for dry whites, sometimes in oak, as in Pessac-Léognan. That gives fuller, waxy wines that can age. In California, Robert Mondavi named his oaked Sauvignon Fumé Blanc in the 1960s, borrowing from Pouilly-Fumé. Chile and South Africa also make fine examples from coastal sites.
Match each region to its Sauvignon Blanc style.
The same grape gives very different wines, from restrained to exuberant.
The Loire gives restrained, mineral Sauvignon
Marlborough gives intense passion fruit and grass
Bordeaux blends it with Sémillon, sometimes in oak
Explain why Riesling expresses place clearly

Riesling is Germany's great grape. In the cool Mosel, on steep slate slopes, it gives light wines, often 7.5 to 9% alcohol, with high acidity and some sweetness. In the Rheingau and Pfalz, warmer and broader, it gives fuller, more often dry wines. Labels may use Prädikat terms, like Kabinett or Spätlese, for ripeness at harvest.

Riesling is rarely oaked, rarely put through malolactic, and is almost never blended. With nothing to mask it, the vineyard speaks clearly: slate, granite and limestone sites give recognisably different wines. Its high acidity, often above 8 g/l, also keeps it fresh for decades, from dry to sweet.
No oak, no blend: pure place
Most German Riesling labelled Kabinett is fermented in new oak.
Not true. Riesling is almost always made without new oak, to keep its pure fruit and acidity. Kabinett refers to ripeness at harvest, not winemaking.

In Alsace, Riesling is mostly dry, fuller and riper, from a dry, sunny valley sheltered by the Vosges. Austria's Wachau and Kamptal make dry, powerful versions on steep terraces above the Danube. Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys give dry, lime-scented wines that develop toast and petrol notes with age.
Match each region to its Riesling.
Each place gives a distinct style, from light and off-dry to powerful and dry.
Germany's Mosel gives light, high-acid, often off-dry Riesling
Alsace, Austria and Australia make mostly dry Riesling
Riesling shows place clearly because it's rarely oaked or blended
Compare Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris styles
Explain the challenges of aromatic grapes

Pinot Gris has pinkish-grey skin. In north-east Italy it is picked early for light, neutral, crisp Pinot Grigio, one of the world's best-selling whites. In Alsace it is picked riper for fuller, richer wines with pear, honey and spice, sometimes off-dry. Oregon makes a middle style. The name on the label usually signals the style.

Gewürztraminer, from the Traminer family of north Italy, has pink skin and intense aromas of lychee, rose and ginger, from compounds called terpenes. It ripens to high sugar and often reaches 14% alcohol with low acidity, which can make it feel heavy. Alsace is its home, from dry to late-harvest sweet.
Lychee and rose, low acidity, high alcohol
Which aroma is most typical of Gewürztraminer?
Lychee and rose are Gewürztraminer's signature, from terpenes. Gooseberry points to Sauvignon Blanc.
Gewürztraminer is a classic with Munster cheese in Alsace, and its exotic perfume suits mildly spiced dishes, especially when a touch of sweetness balances the heat.
Gewürztraminer's main challenge is its naturally low ____.
It ripens to high sugar and alcohol but loses acidity, so growers must pick carefully to keep balance.
Pinot Grigio is light and crisp; Pinot Gris is riper and richer
Gewürztraminer smells of lychee and rose
Aromatic grapes like Gewürztraminer need care to keep acidity
Describe Chenin Blanc's range in the Loire
Explain Sémillon's styles in Bordeaux and Australia

Chenin Blanc has very high acidity and flavours of apple, quince and honey. In the Loire's Anjou and Touraine it makes every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling. Vouvray can be any of these; Savennières is dry and long-lived; Coteaux du Layon is sweet, often from noble rot. South Africa grows more Chenin than any other country.
Chenin: high acid, dry to sweet

Sémillon has thin skins, low acidity and a waxy, lemony texture. Thin skins make it prone to noble rot, the fungus Botrytis cinerea, which shrivels berries and concentrates sugar. That's why it is the main grape of Sauternes. In Australia's Hunter Valley, picked early at about 10 to 11%, it makes lean whites that turn toasty and honeyed after ten years, without oak.
Which styles can Chenin Blanc make in the Loire?
Chenin is made dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling in the Loire. Fortified wines aren't a Loire tradition.

In Bordeaux, Sémillon is blended with Sauvignon Blanc: Sémillon gives body and texture, Sauvignon gives acidity and aroma. South Africa's Chenin often comes from old bush vines in Swartland and Stellenbosch, giving concentrated dry wines, sometimes oaked, that now rank among the country's best.
Sémillon for body, Sauvignon for lift
Why is Sémillon so suited to making Sauternes?
Its thin skins are prone to noble rot
Thin skins let Botrytis cinerea attack, concentrating sugar. That's what makes Sauternes sweet.
Chenin Blanc makes dry, sweet and sparkling wines in the Loire
South Africa grows the most Chenin, often from old vines
Sémillon gives body, ages well in the Hunter and suits noble rot
Describe Viognier and its home in Condrieu

Viognier comes from the northern Rhône, where Condrieu makes full-bodied whites with apricot, peach and violet aromas, low acidity and often 14% alcohol. By the 1960s barely 14 hectares were left; it has since spread to California, Australia and the south of France. In Côte-Rôtie, a little Viognier may be co-fermented with Syrah.
Viognier: apricot and violet, full body

Albariño grows in Rías Baixas, in Galicia, on Spain's wet Atlantic coast. Thick skins resist the damp, and vines are often trained high on pergolas to let air circulate. Its wines are crisp, light to medium-bodied, with lemon, peach and a salty edge. In Portugal it is called Alvarinho, the star grape of Monção e Melgaço in Vinho Verde.
Match each place to its grape.
Viognier belongs to the northern Rhône; Albariño and Alvarinho to the Atlantic north-west of Iberia.

Viognier needs heat to develop its perfume, but must be picked before acidity falls too far. Albariño needs a cool, damp climate and thick skins to stay healthy and fresh. One is generous and soft; the other is bright and salty, a classic with Galician seafood.
Viognier: warm and soft. Albariño: cool and bright.
Why are Albariño vines often trained on high pergolas?
To get more sun on the leaves
To let air circulate and reduce rot in a damp climate
Rías Baixas is very wet. Raising the canopy lets air move through, keeping grapes healthy.
Viognier gives full, perfumed wines, at home in Condrieu
Albariño gives crisp, salty wines on the Atlantic coast
One needs warmth; the other thrives in cool, damp air
Name a classic region for each grape

Grüner Veltliner is Austria's signature grape: crisp, with citrus, green apple and white pepper, from light to powerful in the Wachau. Assyrtiko, from Santorini in Greece, keeps very high acidity even in hot sun, and grows on volcanic soil, giving firm, mineral, citrus wines.
Grüner: white pepper. Assyrtiko: acid and volcanic.

Muscat is a family of grapes that tastes like fresh grapes, thanks to terpenes like linalool and geraniol. It makes light, sweet Moscato d'Asti at 5.5% and rich, fortified wines in southern France. Torrontés, Argentina's white grape, a cross that includes Muscat of Alexandria, gives floral wines in high Salta, up to 3,000 m.
Match each grape to its home.
Each grape has a region where it shows best.

Melon de Bourgogne makes Muscadet, near the Loire's mouth: light, crisp and often aged on its lees, labelled sur lie, which adds texture and a slight spritz. Garganega is the main grape of Soave, in the Veneto, giving almond, lemon and a light texture, and sweet Recioto di Soave from dried grapes.
Muscadet sur lie; Soave from Garganega
Muscadet is made from the Muscat grape.
Not true. Despite the name, Muscadet is made from Melon de Bourgogne. Muscat is a different, aromatic family.
Grüner Veltliner and Assyrtiko are crisp, high-acid whites
Muscat and Torrontés are floral, grape-scented whites
Muscadet comes from Melon; Soave from Garganega

Which compounds give Sauvignon Blanc passion fruit aromas?
Thiols give tropical notes; pyrazines give green ones.
Which grapes are usually made without oak?
Côte de Beaune Chardonnay is classically fermented and aged in oak.
Sémillon's thin skins make it prone to noble rot.
Yes. That's why it is the main grape of Sauternes.
Pinot Grigio in Italy is usually light and crisp, while Pinot ____ in Alsace is richer.
Same grape, Pinot Gris, with the French name linked to the richer style.
Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc change with climate and winemaking
Riesling and Chenin make every style from dry to sweet
Aromatic grapes like Gewürztraminer and Viognier need careful picking
